title: Preparing your documents before touching anything
promise: You'll get your files ready for a search system to understand them: no duplicates, no versions that contradict each other, and a three-line label on each one. By the end you'll have a clean folder and you'll know how many of your documents weren't usable for this.
why: Nuria set up her system with all 340 files exactly as they were. It worked on the first try and she was delighted. A week later she asked it about her commercial contract template and it handed back a penalty clause she had removed in 2019. The old file was still there, named «commercial_contract_GOOD.docx», and the new one was named «commercial_contract_v3_final.docx». The system has no way of knowing which one governs. It found both and answered with whichever it fancied. That wasn't a fault in the software: it was Nuria's filing cabinet, exactly as it was, answering on her behalf.

theory.title: Rubbish in, rubbish out, but better written
theory.text: This is the lesson almost everyone skips and it's the one that decides the outcome. A document search system doesn't judge: it finds what resembles your question and passes it to the model to answer with. If what it finds is out of date, duplicated or half-finished, the answer will come out out of date, duplicated or half-finished, but perfectly written and with an air of certainty. That's worse than having nothing, because it sounds right and because you've already lowered your guard: you built the system precisely so you could stop second-guessing. The real split in the work surprises everyone the first time: in a setup like this, preparing the documents takes around eighty per cent of the time and building the tool the remaining twenty. Every tutorial teaches the twenty, because that's the part you can film and it looks good. The eighty is opening folders and making decisions, and nobody covers it. That's why everyone reaches the end of the tutorial, sees it work with the three sample PDFs, and then gets strange answers with their own.
theory.analogy: It's hiring someone excellent and sitting them in front of a filing cabinet with three versions of every folder, none of them dated, and two boxes of paperwork from a company that no longer exists. However good they are, they'll give you wrong answers. And it isn't their fault.
theory.example: Nuria did the clean-up after the scare. Of 340 files, 96 were duplicates or old versions, 40 were logistics emails without a single criterion inside, and 12 were unreadable scans. She was left with 192. The answers improved more from that afternoon of tidying than from any technical adjustment she made afterwards, and she tried three different tools looking for the blame elsewhere.

theory.title: The four kinds of file that have to go
theory.text: There are four kinds that always get in the way, and you can spot them at a glance without opening much. First, old versions of something that already has a new version. Filing them «just in case» in the same folder doesn't work: either you take them out, or the system reads them as though they still counted as much as the good one. Second, exact duplicates, which turn up everywhere the moment you've ever used a backup or moved things between your computer and the cloud. Third, anything that contains nothing you'd ever query: «received, thanks» emails, acknowledgements, loose screenshots, invoices. Careful with invoices, because they do have data and they're hard to let go of, but it's data to be added up, and we already saw that isn't this system's job. And fourth, scans that are a photo of a piece of paper with no text inside. The computer sees an image, it doesn't see letters. For the system that document is blank however legible it is to you. That fourth kind is the most disorienting, because you'd swear the fact is in there and the system swears it can't find it. You're both right.
theory.example: Quick test for the fourth case: open the PDF and try to select a word with the mouse. If you can, it has text. If the cursor selects a whole rectangle as though it were a photo, it doesn't.

theory.title: Chunking: why it isn't given the whole document
theory.text: When you store a document for searching, it isn't stored in one piece. It's split into chunks of a few paragraphs, and each chunk is stored separately. The reason is simple: when you ask something, what you want back is the paragraph that answers, not a forty-page contract. If the chunks are enormous, every answer arrives with a great deal of filler around it and the model loses track of what matters. If they're tiny, ideas get cut in half and you get half a sentence without the context that explained it: «the deadline shall be fifteen days» with no idea what for. The point that works for normal documents is around half a page, with a small overlap between chunks so no idea gets cut off exactly at the join. Nearly every tool ships with that value set by default and it gets it right. Don't touch it at first: it's the setting most people change and fewest people measure, and changing it without measuring is the definition of losing an afternoon.
theory.analogy: It's how you highlight a textbook. You don't mark the whole chapter or a single word: you mark the paragraph that answers the question. No more, no less.
theory.example: Nuria's 40-page contract is split into about 90 chunks. When she asks about renewals, the system returns the 3 chunks that talk about renewals, not the 40 pages.

theory.title: The three-line label: the trick with the best return
theory.text: This is the detail that separates a setup that works from one that goes so-so, and almost nobody mentions it because it isn't technical and it doesn't look impressive. On each document you put three lines at the top saying what it is, when it's from, and whether it's still in force. Those three lines travel with the document, get chunked with it, and the model reads them. With that it can tell you «this comes from the 2011 criterion, which is still in force» instead of handing you the sentence bare, and you know whether to trust it without opening the file. And above all, when it finds two documents that contradict each other it can look at the dates and tell you, instead of picking one at random and not mentioning there was another. It's about half an hour of work per hundred files if you move quickly, and it completely changes the quality of what you get back. No tool and no setting will give you that improvement for less effort.
theory.example: Nuria wrote three lines at the top of each one like this: «Type: internal circular. Date: March 2011. Status: in force, supersedes the 2008 one.» Since then, when there's a conflict, the answer warns her which one governs instead of choosing.

theory.title: A name that explains itself
theory.text: The file name is passed to the system too, so it's free information that almost everyone wastes. «commercial_contract_v3_final_FINAL_good.docx» tells nobody anything, not the machine and not you in six months. The format that works is always the same: date backwards, type of document, and who or what it's about. With the date backwards — year, month, day — sorting by name sorts you by date, which is what you want ninety per cent of the time. You don't have to rename everything on day one, which is how these things get abandoned: do it with whatever you touch and with the twenty most important ones, and in two weeks it's done without you noticing.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between a shelf with the boxes labelled and one with the boxes merely stacked. Both hold the same things. In one of them you find something without taking them all down.
theory.example: «2019-04-12_commercial-contract_ferreteria-beltran.pdf». You understand it without opening it, it sorts itself, and the system knows when it's from before even reading inside.

theory.title: What stays out for a different reason
theory.text: Some documents are perfectly fine and still shouldn't go in: the ones carrying personal data it isn't your place to put into a system like this. ID numbers, bank accounts, medical reports, payslips with names attached, data about minors. The practical rule, without wading into case law, is this: if that document leaked tomorrow, would you have a serious problem with the person named inside it? If the answer is yes, it stays out until you've thought it through calmly, and that's covered in full in lesson 41. This isn't textbook advice or a formality: it's that these systems get built quickly and enthusiastically, and that's exactly why things get put into them without a second thought. Getting a piece of data back out afterwards is a good deal more awkward than never having put it in, and with some services you can't fully get it out at all.
theory.example: Nuria left out the entire payroll folder and the sick-leave folder, 38 files in all. Her criteria about payroll did go in, written separately by her and without a single name inside. She spent half an hour writing it and saved herself the awkward conversation for good.

tasks.title: Make a copy before touching anything
tasks.action: You're not going to work on your good files. Copy the whole folder somewhere new and name it with today's date: for example «documents-for-ai-2026-09». Copy, don't move. On Windows: right-click the folder, Copy, and paste wherever you like. On Mac, the same with Cmd+C and Cmd+V. Everything you do from here is on the copy. Your originals aren't touched for the rest of the lesson.
tasks.expect: Two folders: the usual one, untouched, and a copy with the date in its name. If your folder is large and the copy takes a while, use the time to do the next task on paper.
tasks.stuck: If you don't have the disk space to duplicate it, don't skip this step: copy only the file types you care about (the PDFs and the Word files, say) instead of the whole folder. Working on the originals is the fastest way to lose something without noticing.

tasks.title: Pull out the duplicates and old versions
tasks.action: Sort the folder by name: duplicates and versions fall next to each other and jump out at you. Create a subfolder called «out» and drag into it everything that's an old version of something that already has a new one, and everything that's repeated. Don't delete it: into the «out» subfolder. When you're torn between two versions of something, check the modified date and keep the newer one; if both look good and you don't know which governs, that doubt is the real problem and it has to be settled now, not left to the system.
tasks.expect: An «out» subfolder with rather more in it than you expected. Twenty to forty per cent leaving is normal. Note how many files you set aside: it's the best measure of what state your filing was in.
tasks.stuck: If you find fifteen versions of the same thing and none clearly governs, open the two most recent side by side and compare. Ten minutes there saves you months of contradictory answers. And if you genuinely can't decide, put both in but give them the label from task 4 saying exactly that: which one you think governs and why.

tasks.title: Set aside anything with no text inside
tasks.action: Open the PDFs that look like scans and try to select a word with the mouse. If you can't, it's a photo: the system will see nothing. Move them to a new subfolder called «no-text». If there are few of them and they matter, they can be fixed: put the PDF through a text-recognition tool and download it converted. If there are many and they aren't critical, leave them set aside and carry on; you can always come back for them.
tasks.expect: Two subfolders set aside («out» and «no-text») and a main folder with documents that genuinely have readable text inside.
tasks.stuck: To decide whether converting is worth it: if that folder holds something you'll actually consult, yes. If they're receipts from eight years ago nobody looks at, no. Conversion works well on printed documents and poorly on handwriting.

tasks.title: Add the three-line label
tasks.where: On each document in the clean folder
tasks.action: Start with the twenty most important, not with all of them. Open each one and write three lines at the very top, before anything else, in this exact format: «Type: [what it is]. Date: [when]. Status: [in force / superseded by X / historical only].» Save. With twenty done you'll already notice the difference; the rest you do as you touch each file. If a document is a PDF and you can't edit it, no matter: put that same information in the file name.
tasks.expect: Twenty documents with three lines at the top. Open them and check. Once the system is running, those lines are what let it tell you «this is from 2011 and still in force» instead of handing you the sentence with no context.
tasks.stuck: If you don't know whether something is still in force, write exactly that: «Status: unconfirmed, review.» That's honest and useful information. What doesn't work is leaving it blank, because then the system has to imagine it, and you know how that ends.

tasks.title: Let the AI help with the names
tasks.action: Renaming by hand is tiring. Make a list of your current file names (on Windows: select all, hold Shift, right-click, «Copy as path»; on Mac: select and Cmd+Alt+C) and paste it into the chat with the prompt below. It gives you back the renamed list and you copy across. Don't let it rename anything itself: it gives you the proposal and you decide.
tasks.prompt:
I'm giving you a list of file names from my work, exactly as they are now. I work in [YOUR SECTOR].

Convert them to the format: YYYY-MM-DD_type-of-document_who-or-what.extension

RULES:
1. All lowercase, no accents, no spaces (use hyphens).
2. If the current name has no date, write NO-DATE in its place. Do not invent one under any circumstances.
3. If you can't tell what a file is about from its name, don't propose anything: write REVIEW next to it and move on.
4. Give it back to me in two columns, current name and proposed name, and nothing else. No introduction and no closing summary.

LIST:
[PASTE YOUR NAMES HERE]
tasks.expect: Two clean columns. The ones that come back as NO-DATE or REVIEW are exactly the ones you need to look at by hand: they tend to be the messiest and often the most important.
tasks.stuck: If it invents dates despite rule 2, say: «You've put in dates that weren't in the list. Do the whole thing again and put NO-DATE on every one that doesn't have it written in.» It's a typical slip and it corrects on the first try when you point it out.

tasks.title: Count what's left and decide whether to carry on
tasks.where: In your note from the previous lesson
tasks.action: Look at the clean folder and note how many documents survived, against how many there were at the start. That number is what will actually go into the system. Now reread the decision you wrote in lesson 30 and check it against the new number, because it changes for a lot of people here.
tasks.expect: A line like: «Started with 340, 192 go in.» If you've dropped below thirty documents, your case has changed: RAG is no longer for you, pasting into the chat is. And that's good news, not a failure.
tasks.stuck: If you're left with far fewer than you thought, it isn't that you did the clean-up badly. It's that your filing had less unique information in it than it looked, which is normal. Better to know now than after building the system.

tasks.title: Sort by size to find the big rubbish
tasks.action: Duplicates show up when you sort by name, but there's other rubbish that only shows up when you sort by size. Switch the folder to detailed list view and sort by size, largest first. Look at the top ten: they're usually presentations full of photos, enormous scanned PDFs and videos that snuck in. Now sort smallest first: anything under 5 KB is almost always an empty file, a shortcut or a leftover.
tasks.expect: Two short lists and a few more files for the «out» folder. The enormous ones are usually text-free scans, so you probably set them aside already; the tiny ones are near-certain rubbish.
tasks.stuck: If a large file turns out to matter, don't set it aside: flag it for text recognition. Size doesn't decide, it only tells you where to look first.

tasks.title: Write down what governs when two documents disagree
tasks.action: During the clean-up you'll hit contradictions you can't resolve. Instead of leaving them, write down the rule you use without thinking and have never put in writing. For example: «between an internal circular and an email, the circular governs»; «between two documents of the same type, the most recent governs»; «signed beats spoken». Three or four rules is enough.
tasks.expect: Three or four lines. This file goes into the system later as another document, and it's one of the highest-return ones: it gives the model a way to resolve the conflicts it finds, instead of leaving it to choose.
tasks.stuck: If you have no clear rules, it's because until now you resolved them case by case. Write down the last three times you did and what you decided: the rule is underneath.

tasks.title: Check the clean-up with five manual searches
tasks.action: Before calling the clean-up done, test it the way the system will use it. Take five things you know are written in your documents and search for them with your computer's search inside the clean folder. On Windows, type in the folder's search box; on Mac, Cmd+F inside the folder. Note whether each one appears, in how many files, and whether any of those files is one you set aside.
tasks.expect: Five searches with their results. If something important appears only in a file you'd sent to «out», bring it back. If something appears in six different files, you have a contradiction waiting there: check which governs and note it.
tasks.stuck: If your computer's search doesn't look inside PDFs, indexing isn't switched on. Don't fight it: open the five files you think hold the fact and check by eye. Five files take five minutes.

matters: That preparing the documents is 80% of the work, and it's where almost everyone fails.
That two versions of the same document with no date or status guarantee contradictory answers.
That a scan with no text inside is invisible to the system, however clearly you can read it.
That three lines of label per document return more than any technical adjustment afterwards.
ignore: The exact chunk size. The factory value gets it right for normal documents.
Converting everything to a single format. The tools in this course read PDF, Word and text without trouble.
Automatic deduplication tools. Sorting by name and looking is plenty at this scale.
canDo: Recognise the four kinds of file that get in the way and set them aside.
Add a status label that prevents contradictory answers.
Check whether a PDF really has text or is a photo.
Rename hundreds of files with the AI's help without it inventing dates.
cantDo: Query the documents yet: that's lesson 32.
Have it decide for you which version governs when both are good. That's your call.
Include documents with sensitive personal data: that waits for lesson 41.
Recover text from a bad or handwritten scan.
words: Splitting each document into fragments of a few paragraphs so only the part that answers can be returned.
Having each chunk repeat a little of the previous one, so no idea gets cut off exactly at the join.
The data about the document: type, date, status. The three-line label, in technical terms.
Text recognition. Turns the photo of a page into letters a computer can read.
Whether a document still governs or another one superseded it. Without this, the system can't resolve contradictions.
next: With the folder clean and labelled, in lesson 32 you upload it to a tool and ask it your first question. You'll see the whole thing working in under twenty minutes, and without writing a single line of code.
